title: The Gopis Perform the Katyayani Vow
story:
It was still dark when they left their houses. The young girls of Vrindavan went down to the river in the cold, before the first color of dawn touched the water, and they slipped into the Yamuna while the stars were still out. This was not a game. It was a vow.

The verses call them kumaryas — young girls, not yet married — and what they set themselves to do was a thing of discipline. All through the first month of winter they rose while it was still night and went down to the water, every morning, and their mothers knew and said nothing. The river was cold, the air colder, and still they went. The winter had set its teeth into Vraja; the ground was hard underfoot, and the water, when they entered it, took the breath away. But the vow had been made, and a vow begun in winter is not a thing to break because the morning is cold.

At the water's edge they made an image of the goddess Katyayani, and they worshipped her the way a house is worshipped — with fragrant paste and garlands and offerings, with incense and a burning lamp held steady in the dark. The paste was rubbed into the image, the garlands hung about it, the offerings laid before it, and through it all the little flame of the lamp stood between them and the dark, so that the goddess they prayed to was never without light.

And to her they spoke one prayer, the same prayer every day. "O Katyayani," they said, calling her the great power, the great yogini, the supreme ruler, "make Nanda's son my husband."

That was the whole of it. There was no other request in the vow. The verses are plain about this: for a month the young girls performed it, their minds fixed on Krishna, with not a single other wish to dilute it. They did not come to the goddess with the long list of wants that most prayers carry; they came with one.

They went together. The verses say they rose at dawn and linked their arms with one another as they went, girl beside girl, so that the cold and the dark were shared between them. There is something brave in that detail — the way they held each other against the morning. None of them went alone; none of them had to carry the whole weight of the vow by herself.

They did not ask for riches, or long life, or good fortune, or any of the things a family might pray for on a daughter's behalf. They asked for him. And the goddess they chose to ask was Katyayani, the one the verses call the great illusion and the great yogini — as if they understood, even then, that what they were asking for would not come to them by any ordinary road.

Day after day the pattern held, and the month did not break it. What began as a private wish became a shared discipline, and the river saw the same small procession each dawn — the girls, the cold water, the lamp, the image, the one request. Nothing in the verses suggests they wavered or grew tired, only that they kept at it, morning after morning, with the name of Nanda's son on their lips and the goddess before them. By the time the sun was fully up they would be dressed and turning for home, and the day would begin as if nothing had happened — but the vow was one day nearer its end, and the river had one more morning of their prayer to keep.
reflection: The vow's force lies in what it leaves out. There is no petition for safety or prosperity, only the single, unhedged request — Nanda's son. And they ask together, arms linked, so that the longing itself becomes something shared rather than borne alone.
next_story_tease: But Krishna would soon find them at the river, and what he did there would test the vow they had made.
hero_scene: The young gopis standing in the cold water of the Yamuna before dawn, arms linked, worshipping an image of the goddess Katyayani by incense and lamplight as the first light touches the river.
